chief_complaint: solid food getting stuck in my chest and slow swallowing for 2 years
hpi_details: 2-year history of intermittent, predictable dysphagia specifically to solid foods, particularly dry meats, chicken, and bread. Requires drinking large amounts of water with every meal to wash food down. Had one episode of acute food bolus impaction requiring emergency room observation last summer. Denies weight loss, pain on swallowing (odynophagia), or progressive liquid dysphagia.
ideas: thinks he has a narrow food pipe because of his childhood allergies and asthma
concerns: anxious every time he eats at restaurants in case he chokes in public
expectations: wants a camera scope to check the throat and an inhaler or steroid therapy to calm the swelling
pmh: moderate asthma, allergic rhinitis, childhood atopic eczema
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks socially, software developer, allergic to peanuts and shellfish

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Eosinophilic Oesophagitis (EoE) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Diagnostic OGD with multi-level oesophageal biopsies, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: solid food getting stuck in my chest and slow swallowing for 2 years

Key HPI features: 2-year history of intermittent, predictable dysphagia specifically to solid foods, particularly dry meats, chicken, and bread. Requires drinking large amounts of water with every meal to wash food down. Had one episode of acute food bolus impaction requiring emergency room observation last summer. Denies weight loss, pain on swallowing (odynophagia), or progressive liquid dysphagia.

Objective/Exam findings: Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) showing classic endoscopic features: oesophageal rings ('trachealization'), linear furrows, white exudates/plaques, or crepe-paper mucosa. Oesophageal mucosal biopsies taken from proximal and distal oesophagus (>15 eosinophils per high-power field confirms diagnosis).
Relevant background/PMH: moderate asthma, allergic rhinitis, childhood atopic eczema
Current medications: budesonide/formoterol inhaler BID, cetirizine 10mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Eosinophilic Oesophagitis (EoE).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: A prior food bolus impaction requiring emergency care — a marker of significant narrowing.
management_principles: Diagnostic OGD with multi-level oesophageal biopsies
Initiate topical swallowed corticosteroid therapy (e.g., swallowed fluticasone inhaler or budesonide orodispersible tablets - Jorveza) or high-dose proton pump inhibitor trial (PPI-responsive EoE)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 27M with strong atopic triad presents with 2-year solid-food dysphagia, history of food impaction, and water-assisted swallowing. No weight loss.
reference_soap.objective: Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) showing classic endoscopic features: oesophageal rings ('trachealization'), linear furrows, white exudates/plaques, or crepe-paper mucosa. Oesophageal mucosal biopsies taken from proximal and distal oesophagus (>15 eosinophils per high-power field confirms diagnosis).
reference_soap.assessment: Eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE). DDx: gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture, achalasia, Schatzki ring, oesophageal motility disorder.
reference_soap.plan: Diagnostic OGD with multi-level oesophageal biopsies. Initiate topical swallowed corticosteroid therapy (e.g., swallowed fluticasone inhaler or budesonide orodispersible tablets - Jorveza) or high-dose proton pump inhibitor trial (PPI-responsive EoE). Refer to dietitian for consideration of six-food elimination diet. Instruct on avoiding chewing food inadequately.

learning_objectives: Link chronic solid-food dysphagia and food bolus impaction in young adults with an underlying atopic phenotype (asthma/eczema/rhinitis)
Outline the endoscopic features ('trachealization' rings, furrows, exudates) and histological criteria (>15 eosinophils/HPF) of EoE
Explain the novel administration method of swallowed topical corticosteroids (e.g., spraying inhaler onto tongue and swallowing without inhaling)
Discuss dietary exclusion strategies (six-food elimination diet) alongside pharmacological management

teaching.one_liner: Allergic inflammation fills the oesophagus with eosinophils, narrowing it so solid food — especially dry meat and bread — repeatedly sticks, often in people with other allergies or asthma.
differentials: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture
red_flags: A prior food bolus impaction requiring emergency care — a marker of significant narrowing

must_ask.say: Is it specific solid foods that get stuck, like meat or bread, while liquids go down fine?
Have you ever had food get completely stuck, needing a hospital visit?
Do you need to drink a lot of water with meals to help the food go down?
Do you have asthma, hay fever, or any food allergies?
Is it just difficult to swallow, or does it also hurt when you do?
Have you lost any weight because of this?

history.answer: For the past two years, solid food keeps getting stuck in my chest when I eat.
It started about two years ago, and it happens every so often rather than getting steadily worse every day.
I can start the swallow easily, but a few seconds later the food gets stuck right in the middle of my chest.
It only happens with dense solids like dry chicken, steak, and crusty bread, whereas water and liquids go down with no issue at all.
Last summer a piece of chicken got completely stuck and I had to go to the emergency room, and at home I always have to drink big gulps of water to wash food down.
I eat very slowly, cut my food into tiny pieces, and chew each bite a lot before swallowing.
No, I don't choke, cough, have food come out of my nose, or get chest infections.
No, food never comes back up undigested, and I haven't noticed bad breath or a gurgling sound in my neck.
No, it doesn't hurt when I swallow; it just feels mechanically stuck in my chest.
No, I don't have chronic heartburn or sour acid rising up into my mouth.
No, I haven't had any squeezing, tight, or crushing chest pain.
My appetite is fine and my weight has stayed steady around 70 kilograms.
No, I have never thrown up blood or noticed black, tarry bowel movements.
No, my voice sounds normal and hasn't become hoarse.
No slurred speech, facial weakness, drooping eyelids, double vision, or weakness in my limbs.
Yes, I have moderate asthma and allergic rhinitis, had eczema as a kid, and I'm allergic to peanuts and shellfish.
I always take my pills standing or sitting up with a full glass of water, and I don't have immune deficiency.
No, my fingers don't turn white or blue in the cold, and my skin hasn't gotten tight.
No, I haven't felt any lumps, bumps, or swelling in my neck.
I wonder if my food pipe is narrowed or swollen because of all my childhood allergies and asthma.
I get really anxious eating at restaurants because I'm terrified of choking in front of other people.
I was hoping to get an endoscopy camera to check my food pipe and maybe get an inhaler or steroid medicine to calm the swelling.
Just my asthma, allergic rhinitis, and the childhood eczema; no other medical conditions.
I've never had surgery, just that one emergency room visit last summer when food was stuck.
I use a budesonide and formoterol inhaler twice a day and take a cetirizine 10 milligram allergy tablet once daily.
No allergies to medicines, just food allergies to peanuts and shellfish.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink socially, usually just one or two beers on the weekend.
I work as a software engineer and live alone in an apartment.
My mother has asthma and eczema, but nobody in my family has had throat or stomach cancer.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-nourished young male sitting comfortably in no acute distress, with normal hydration status.
Oropharynx is clear without mucosal erythema, white plaques, or ulcerations; dentition is intact.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpated.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, and moves freely with deglutition without nodules.
Cranial nerves IX, X, and XII intact; palate elevates symmetrically, tongue protrudes midline, and water swallowing test produces no coughing or wet voice.
Breath sounds are clear bilaterally with no wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, non-distended, with no epigastric masses or guarding.
Liver and spleen are non-palpable below the costal margins without hepatosplenomegaly.
Normal skin turgor with no active eczema, erythema, sclerodactyly, or rash.
